# Results — Study 145 (Home-Bias) on real tape

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). Daily log-returns for
SPY (US large-cap), EFA (MSCI EAFE developed ex-US), EEM (MSCI Emerging Markets),
from the shared `cross_asset_etfs.parquet` cache (Yahoo Finance total-return prices).
Blend = 60% SPY / 25% EFA / 15% EEM, annual calendar-year rebalancing.
As-of **2026-06-14**; window driven by EEM inception (2003-04-14).*

## Per-asset statistics (2003-04-15 – 2026-06-11)

| Ticker | Ann. Return | Ann. Vol | Sharpe | Max Drawdown |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY (US) | **+11.0%** | 18.6% | **+0.59** | −59.6% |
| EFA (dev ex-US) | +7.9% | 20.7% | +0.38 | −65.9% |
| EEM (emerging) | +9.7% | 27.0% | +0.36 | −73.4% |

The US dominated on all three axes: higher return, lower vol, higher Sharpe, smaller
drawdown than either international leg.

## Portfolio comparison: US-only vs global blend

| Portfolio | Ann. Return | Ann. Vol | Sharpe | Max Drawdown | n |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **US only (SPY)** | **+10.97%** | **18.6%** | **+0.591** | **−59.6%** | 5,827 |
| Global blend (60/25/15) | +10.01% | 19.4% | +0.515 | −62.5% | 5,827 |

The global blend *underperforms* US-only on **every axis**: lower return (−0.96%/yr),
higher volatility (+0.89%), lower Sharpe (−0.077), and *deeper* maximum drawdown
(−62.5% vs −59.6%). The diversification "free lunch" is absent in this period.

## Mean excess return of blend over US-only

| Mean (bps/day) | SE (HAC) | HAC t-stat | n |
|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **−0.38** | 0.33 | **−1.17** | 5,827 |

The blend underperforms by **−0.38 bps/day** (≈ −0.96%/yr), HAC t = **−1.17** —
statistically consistent with zero given the sample length. The point estimate is
negative but not significant: it would take a substantially longer sample or a larger
effect to distinguish it from noise.

## Sharpe difference (blend − US): block-bootstrap 95% CI

| Statistic | Value |
|---|--:|
| Point estimate (Δ Sharpe) | **−0.077** |
| 95% CI low | −0.165 |
| 95% CI high | +0.012 |
| Frac. resamples where blend < US | **95%** |

The bootstrap CI almost entirely sits below zero. 95% of block-bootstrap resamples
show the blend below US-only. The diversification benefit, if it exists at all,
is too small to distinguish from noise in 23 years of data, and the point estimate
runs the wrong way.

## Correlation structure

### 63-day rolling correlation (SPY vs partners)

| Pair | Min | Mean | Max |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY–EFA | 0.40 | **0.83** | 0.97 |
| SPY–EEM | 0.15 | **0.76** | 0.97 |

International equity correlations with the US have been **high and rising** since the
2000s. Mean rolling correlations of 0.83 (EFA) and 0.76 (EEM) leave little room for
the variance-reduction benefit that makes international diversification work in theory.

### Crisis vs calm correlations (bottom 20% SPY days = crisis)

| Partner | Corr crisis | Corr calm | Δ (crisis − calm) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| EFA | 0.823 | 0.811 | +0.012 |
| EEM | 0.736 | 0.729 | +0.007 |

Correlations are nearly **identical in crisis and calm periods** for this linear-model
world. On real data, correlations between equity markets spike dramatically in crashes
(2008, 2020), which is exactly when the diversification is most needed and least present.

## Rebalancing cost note

Annual rebalancing has low turnover: the blend holds three ETFs drifting apart over a
year; the annual rebalancing trade is typically <5% of portfolio notional. At 2 bps
round-trip (liquid ETFs), cost drag is ~0.1 bps/yr — negligible relative to the
observed return gap.

## Synthetic positive control (from run_synthetic_demo.py)

On a synthetic panel, the global blend improves Sharpe *only* when: (a) correlations
are low (≤0.4) **and** (b) US and international have equal expected returns. Neither
condition holds on the real 2003-2026 tape: correlations averaged 0.83 (EFA) and US
dominated by +3.1%/yr. The engine correctly returns near-zero or negative Sharpe
improvement in the US-dominant, high-correlation regime.

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE.** The global blend's Sharpe (0.515) is *below* US-only (0.591); the
  mean excess return is −0.38 bps/day (HAC t = −1.17). No statistically significant
  Sharpe improvement; 95% of bootstrap resamples favour US-only.
- **Diversification: real but overridden.** International equity did reduce concentration
  risk marginally, but rising correlations (SPY-EFA mean 0.83) and US structural
  outperformance (+3.1%/yr) overwhelmed any variance-reduction benefit.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** Blend Sharpe < US-only at zero cost, with higher vol and
  deeper drawdown. There is nothing to trade here; the naive claim (diversification
  improves risk-adjusted return) is empirically false for this period.
- **Correlation claim: confirmed but unhelpfully.** Crisis-period correlations are
  marginally higher than calm, confirming that international equity offers no refuge
  precisely when diversification is needed most.
